moments.title: Turing's 'On Computable Numbers'
moments.body:
A 24-year-old graduate student writes a paper introducing a universal machine that can simulate any other.

In the same paper, Turing proves the halting problem is undecidable; no algorithm can determine in advance whether an arbitrary program will terminate.

quote.text: We may compare a man in the process of computing a real number to a machine which is only capable of a finite number of conditions.

moments.takeaway: The Turing machine became the theoretical foundation of computer science.

moments.title: Von Neumann architecture
moments.body:
The First Draft of a Report on the EDVAC describes a machine where program instructions and data share the same memory.

The stored-program design will dominate computing for decades.
moments.takeaway: A single architectural choice in 1945 shaped almost every subsequent computer.

moments.title: The Manchester Baby runs
moments.body: The Small-Scale Experimental Machine becomes the first stored-program computer to execute a program. It runs for 52 minutes calculating the highest proper factor of a number.
moments.takeaway: Theory met hardware in a university laboratory, not a corporate lab.

now.title: Computing today
now.body: Every computer is, in principle, a Turing machine. The halting problem still has no general solution. New limits (quantum supremacy claims, P vs NP) extend the conversation Turing started.
now.open_questions: Does P equal NP? Can quantum computers solve problems classical computers cannot solve in polynomial time?

items.reflection: Turing was prosecuted for his sexuality in 1952 and died in 1954. How should the history of a field treat the people who built it but were excluded from it?

moments.title: ARPANET sends its first message
moments.body:
On 29 October 1969, Charley Kline tries to log in from UCLA to Stanford. The system crashes after the letters 'L' and 'O'.

The network grows to four nodes by December.
moments.takeaway: The internet's foundational moment was a partial failure.

moments.title: TCP described
moments.body: The paper 'A Protocol for Packet Network Intercommunication' describes what becomes TCP/IP. The protocol becomes the basis of internetworking.
moments.takeaway: Decoupling networks from their physical layer enabled the open internet.

moments.title: Web proposal at CERN
moments.body: Berners-Lee's March 1989 proposal addresses how to share documents across a heterogeneous research organisation. The first web server runs in 1990.
moments.takeaway: Major shifts can begin as internal solutions to specific organisational problems.

now.title: Networks today
now.body: Roughly 5 billion people now use the internet. Concerns over consolidation, surveillance and resilience shape policy debates around net neutrality and platform regulation.
now.open_questions: How should the internet's open architecture be preserved as more layers concentrate among a few providers?

items.reflection: The internet was built on military funding for academic purposes and then commercialised, with each transition shaping who held power over it.

moments.title: New Directions in Cryptography
moments.who: Whitfield Diffie and Martin Hellman, Stanford
moments.body: The paper publicly introduces the concept of public-key cryptography, enabling secure communication without prior shared secrets.
moments.takeaway: A theoretical breakthrough made secure communication on open networks possible.

moments.title: RSA published
moments.body: The RSA algorithm provides the first widely deployed public-key system whose security rests on integer factorisation.
moments.takeaway: Mathematical hardness assumptions translated into deployable infrastructure.

moments.title: GCHQ reveals earlier discovery
moments.who: James Ellis, Clifford Cocks and Malcolm Williamson
moments.body: GCHQ discloses that British cryptographers had independently developed analogous public-key methods in the early 1970s, classified at the time.
moments.takeaway: Public scientific history may differ from classified records.

now.title: Cryptography today
now.body: RSA, elliptic-curve and lattice-based methods all underpin internet security. NIST is standardising post-quantum cryptography in anticipation of large-scale quantum computers.
now.open_questions: Will any current public-key algorithm survive practical quantum computing? How is cryptographic agility built into infrastructure?

items.reflection: The same mathematics secures messages and breaks them. Cryptography sits at the intersection of national security and personal privacy.

moments.title: Rosenblatt's perceptron
moments.body:
Rosenblatt's perceptron is the first practical artificial neural network for pattern classification.

Minsky and Papert's 1969 book Perceptrons argues that single-layer networks have fundamental limits, contributing to a first 'AI winter'.
moments.takeaway: Optimism and limit-results have cycled through AI's history.

moments.title: Backpropagation widely adopted
moments.body:
The paper popularises the backpropagation algorithm, allowing efficient training of multi-layer networks.

The method was earlier described by others (Werbos, 1974).
moments.takeaway: Algorithmic improvements without sufficient data and compute can sit unused for decades.

moments.title: AlexNet wins ImageNet
moments.body: AlexNet's deep convolutional network reduces error on the ImageNet competition by a large margin, triggering the modern deep-learning era.
moments.takeaway: The combination of GPUs, large datasets and deep architectures restarted the field.

now.title: AI today
now.body: Large language models and generative systems are deployed across industries. Compute-scaling laws, energy use and governance frameworks are under active debate.
now.open_questions: Will scaling current architectures continue to produce capability gains? How should generative systems be regulated across jurisdictions?

items.reflection: AI's history shows how labels ('intelligent', 'understanding') travel and stretch as the underlying systems change.

moments.title: Babbage describes the Analytical Engine
moments.body: Babbage publishes the first detailed description of his Analytical Engine — a mechanical, general-purpose, programmable computer using punched cards adapted from the Jacquard loom. It would have had a 'store' (memory), 'mill' (CPU), conditional branching, and looping.
moments.takeaway: A general-purpose programmable computer was theoretically described 109 years before the first one ran.

moments.title: Lovelace's notes on the Engine
moments.body: Lovelace translates Luigi Menabrea's French paper on the Analytical Engine and adds 'Notes' three times its length. Note G describes an algorithm to compute Bernoulli numbers — often cited as the first published algorithm intended for a machine. Lovelace also speculates the Engine could compose music or manipulate symbols beyond numbers.

quote.text: The Analytical Engine has no pretensions whatever to originate anything. It can do whatever we know how to order it to perform.
quote.attrib: Ada Lovelace, Notes on the Analytical Engine, 1843

moments.takeaway: Lovelace grasped that programmability meant the machine was about manipulating symbols, not just calculation.

now.title: Mechanical computing today
now.body: Babbage's Difference Engine No. 2 was finally built by the Science Museum, London, in 1991 (calculating part) and 2002 (printer) — and worked. The Analytical Engine was never built. Ada (the language, 1980) is named for Lovelace; the 'Ada Lovelace Day' second Tuesday of October celebrates women in STEM.
now.open_questions: Why did it take until the 1940s to realise mechanically what Babbage described? Funding, manufacturing tolerances and the absence of a clear market all played roles.

items.reflection: Computing has always had visionaries who saw the destination before the technology existed to take them there. Lovelace's reach beyond pure calculation prefigures the symbolic-AI debates of a century later.

moments.title: An Investigation of the Laws of Thought
moments.body: Boole publishes his second work on symbolic logic. He shows that logical statements can be manipulated algebraically using a small set of operations (AND, OR, NOT) and that this algebra is internally consistent.
moments.takeaway: Reasoning is reduced to algebra — a precondition for electronic computing a century later.

moments.title: Shannon's master's thesis
moments.body: Shannon's master's thesis 'A Symbolic Analysis of Relay and Switching Circuits' shows that Boolean algebra can be implemented in electrical relay circuits — the foundation of digital logic design.
moments.takeaway: Boole's algebra and electrical engineering meet, making digital computing physically realisable.

now.title: Boolean logic today
now.body: Every digital circuit, every CPU operation, every database query (WHERE clauses) and every program control flow uses Boolean logic. Shannon's other major work, 'A Mathematical Theory of Communication' (1948), founded information theory.
now.open_questions: Are there practical extensions beyond binary? Multi-valued logic, fuzzy logic and quantum computing all explore alternatives — none have replaced two-valued Boolean logic as the substrate of digital systems.

items.reflection: An Irish mathematician working on the foundations of logic in 1854 built the algebraic framework on which all modern computing rests. Pure mathematics often turns out to be applied mathematics on a long lag.

moments.title: A Relational Model of Data for Large Shared Data Banks
moments.body: Codd publishes his foundational paper in Communications of the ACM, proposing that data should be organised in normalised tables (relations) with no hierarchical or network structure exposed to applications.
moments.takeaway: Decoupling logical data structure from physical storage made databases dramatically more useful and portable.

moments.title: Oracle, IBM DB2 ship relational databases
moments.body: Oracle V2 ships in 1979 as the first commercial relational database. IBM DB2 follows in 1983. By the late 1980s the relational model is dominant in business computing.
moments.takeaway: Theoretical advance translated into commercial product within a decade — driven by the rise of standalone application servers and SQL standardisation (ISO/IEC 9075, 1987).

now.title: Relational databases today
now.body: Relational databases remain the workhorse of business computing. Open-source options (PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite) match or exceed commercial systems for many workloads. NoSQL alternatives emerged from 2009 for scale and flexibility but did not replace relational — most large organisations run both.
now.open_questions: How should databases be designed for hybrid transactional/analytical workloads (HTAP)? Cloud-native database architectures (Aurora, Spanner, Snowflake) are redrawing the boundaries.

items.reflection: Codd, who won the 1981 Turing Award, was an academic at heart and disagreed with IBM's eventual SQL implementation (he preferred his own tuple calculus). The product won; the theory was honoured.

moments.title: ARPANET goes live
moments.who: BBN, UCLA, Stanford, UCSB, University of Utah
moments.body: On 29 October 1969, the first ARPANET message is sent between UCLA and Stanford Research Institute. By December 1969 the network has four nodes. The packet-switching design (Paul Baran 1964, Donald Davies 1965) eliminates the single point of failure of circuit-switched networks.
moments.takeaway: A research network funded by the US Department of Defense becomes the technical seed of the global internet.

moments.title: ARPANET adopts TCP/IP
moments.body: On 1 January 1983 ARPANET cuts over from NCP to TCP/IP, making it possible to connect different networks transparently. The cutover ('flag day') was a coordinated effort across all connected systems.
moments.takeaway: Standardising on TCP/IP made internetworking — networks of networks — possible. The internet name dates from this period.

now.title: The internet today
now.body: Around 5 billion people use the internet. The original ARPANET design (open, distributed, end-to-end) has been partly eroded by NAT, CDNs and platform consolidation. ICANN (1998) coordinates names and addresses; the IETF still produces the technical standards.
now.open_questions: How can the open, end-to-end internet architecture be preserved as a few large operators concentrate traffic and DNS?

items.reflection: The decision to publish ARPANET protocols openly, rather than as proprietary military systems, shaped half a century of technology development. Open standards have an outsized effect on long-run outcomes.

moments.title: C is developed at Bell Labs
moments.body: Ritchie develops C as a systems programming language for the PDP-11, derived from B (Ken Thompson) and BCPL. C combines low-level access (pointers, bit operations) with structured-programming constructs.
moments.takeaway: A language designed for writing operating systems became the lingua franca of systems programming for the next 50 years.

moments.title: K&R: The C Programming Language
moments.body: The first edition of 'The C Programming Language' becomes both the de facto language reference and a model for technical writing. The 'Hello, World' program example starts a tradition that survives today.
moments.takeaway: The book sets a standard for concise technical exposition that has influenced programming documentation ever since.

moments.title: ANSI C standard
moments.body: C is formally standardised (C89/C90). The standardisation process resolved ambiguities and made portable C realistic. Later revisions: C99, C11, C17, C23.
moments.takeaway: Standardisation extended C's life and portability for another four decades.

now.title: C today
now.body: C remains foundational: Linux, Windows kernels, embedded systems, databases, language runtimes (CPython, V8). Most other languages compile to or interoperate with C. Memory-safety concerns are gradually pushing systems code toward Rust, but the existing C codebase is enormous and persistent.
now.open_questions: Can the world's installed base of C/C++ systems code be migrated to memory-safe languages? Government agencies (NSA 2022, CISA 2023) have begun publicly recommending this.

items.reflection: Two engineers at Bell Labs built a language that runs almost every operating system you'll ever use, mostly without explicit decision by their employers.

moments.title: Unix begins on a PDP-7
moments.who: Ken Thompson, Dennis Ritchie, Bell Labs
moments.body: After Bell Labs withdraws from the Multics project, Thompson begins a smaller operating system on a spare PDP-7. The first version of Unix supports file system, fork/exec, and a shell.
moments.takeaway: A minor side project replaces the larger system it diverged from.

moments.title: Unix rewritten in C
moments.body: Unix is rewritten in C, making it portable between hardware architectures. This is unusual at a time when operating systems were tied to specific machines.
moments.takeaway: Portability turned Unix from a single-machine project into a transferable platform.

moments.title: BSD and Linux fork the lineage
moments.body: Berkeley Software Distribution (BSD) and Linux (kernel 1991, paired with GNU userland) carry the Unix design into open source. macOS (2001) is built on a BSD-derived kernel (Darwin).
moments.takeaway: Open implementations of Unix design now dominate servers, mobile (Android on Linux, iOS on Darwin) and even desktops to some extent.

now.title: Unix philosophy
now.body: 'Write programs that do one thing and do it well; write programs to work together; write programs that handle text streams' (Doug McIlroy) — these principles shape modern Unix systems. Microservices, container architectures and shell pipelines all share intellectual ancestry with early Unix.
now.open_questions: Is the Unix philosophy still applicable to very large-scale distributed systems? Modern cloud architectures combine Unix-style composition with non-Unix orchestration.

items.reflection: Most of the world's computing — almost all servers, all Android phones, all Apple devices — runs systems descended from a 1969 side project at Bell Labs.

moments.title: BASIC at Dartmouth
moments.body: Kemeny and Kurtz design BASIC (Beginner's All-purpose Symbolic Instruction Code) to teach non-STEM students programming on the Dartmouth Time-Sharing System. Simple syntax, line numbers, immediate execution.
moments.takeaway: Programming was designed for beginners deliberately — not all language design defaults to systems programmers.

moments.title: Altair BASIC
moments.who: Bill Gates and Paul Allen, soon to form Microsoft
moments.body: Gates and Allen write Altair BASIC for the MITS Altair 8800 — the first microcomputer to capture hobbyist attention. The product launches Microsoft.
moments.takeaway: Software for personal computers became a business in itself.

moments.title: BBC Micro and home computing
moments.body: BBC Micro (1981) ships with BBC BASIC and becomes the standard in UK schools as part of the BBC Computer Literacy Project. ZX Spectrum (1982), Commodore 64 (1982), Apple II all let users boot into BASIC. A generation of British and American programmers learn on these machines.
moments.takeaway: The BBC Micro alone went into around 80% of UK schools — a deliberate national programme to teach computing.

now.title: Programming for beginners today
now.body: Scratch (MIT, 2007), Python (now the default teaching language), micro:bit (BBC, 2015), the Raspberry Pi (2012) all carry forward the idea that programming should be accessible. The UK's 2014 curriculum reform reintroduced computing as a core subject; BBC's 2015 'Make It Digital' echoed the 1981 initiative.
now.open_questions: Does teaching block-based programming (Scratch) before text-based help or hinder later learning? Empirical evidence is mixed.

items.reflection: BASIC's name reflects an explicit choice: programming was for beginners too. The current resurgence of teaching computing in schools is part of a longer arc whose previous peak was the 1980s home computer boom.

moments.title: Information Management: A Proposal
moments.body: Berners-Lee's March 1989 proposal addresses the loss of information at CERN as researchers come and go. His supervisor Mike Sendall calls it 'vague but exciting' and approves time for prototyping.
moments.takeaway: A proposal that became the foundation of the web was initially described as 'vague but exciting'.

moments.title: First web browser and server
moments.body: By December 1990 Berners-Lee has written the first web browser (WorldWideWeb, on a NeXT machine), the first web server (CERN httpd), and the first web page (info.cern.ch). The HTTP, HTML and URL specifications all date from this work.
moments.takeaway: The web's foundational technologies were built largely by one person in months.

moments.title: CERN releases the web royalty-free
moments.body: On 30 April 1993, CERN puts the underlying technology in the public domain. Mosaic (NCSA, 1993) and then Netscape (1994) bring the web to a mass audience.
moments.takeaway: The decision not to patent or licence the web was decisive in its explosive uptake.

now.title: The web today
now.body: The web is the dominant interface for most computing. HTML, HTTP and URL have all evolved (HTTP/2, HTTP/3 over QUIC; HTML5; URLs extended with WebSockets, ServiceWorkers). The W3C (1994) and WHATWG (2004) coordinate standards. Berners-Lee runs the Solid project (2018) to give users more control over their data.
now.open_questions: Can the web's original decentralisation be restored as platforms concentrate user attention and data?

items.reflection: An internal documentation problem at a physics lab became the most-used application of the internet. The decision to keep the technology open mattered more than any technical choice.

moments.title: Linus announces Linux
moments.body: On 25 August 1991, 21-year-old Torvalds posts to comp.os.minix: 'I'm doing a (free) operating system (just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu) for 386(486) AT clones.' Version 0.01 is released in September; 1.0 follows in 1994.

quote.text: Just a hobby, won't be big and professional like gnu.

moments.takeaway: An accurate prediction would have been considered grandiose at the time.

moments.title: Open Source Initiative founded
moments.who: Eric Raymond, Bruce Perens and others
moments.body: The Open Source Initiative is founded to promote a business-friendly framing of free software. Netscape releases Mozilla source code the same year. IBM commits to Linux in 1998.
moments.takeaway: Open source moves from movement to industrial strategy as commercial firms adopt it.

now.title: Linux today
now.body: Linux runs essentially all of the world's 500 fastest supercomputers, the majority of web servers, Android (3 billion+ active devices), and substantial fractions of cloud infrastructure. The kernel has had over 22,000 contributors. Linux Foundation hosts not just Linux but Kubernetes, Node.js and many other core projects.
now.open_questions: How sustainable is a model where corporate interests fund most kernel development while individual maintainers remain unpaid?

items.reflection: An undergraduate project in Helsinki became the most widely deployed operating system kernel in history. Open licences and global collaboration made it possible.

moments.title: BackRub at Stanford
moments.who: Larry Page and Sergey Brin, Stanford
moments.body: Page and Brin's PhD project 'BackRub' analyses the link structure of the web. Their PageRank algorithm ranks pages by treating links as votes weighted by the importance of the linking page — a recursive definition with elegant fixed-point properties.
moments.takeaway: Web search before Google was largely keyword matching; the breakthrough was recognising that the link graph itself contained ranking signal.

moments.title: Google incorporated
moments.body: Google is incorporated on 4 September 1998 in a Menlo Park garage. The original investment cheque from Andy Bechtolsheim arrived for Google Inc. before the company existed; it was held for two weeks waiting for incorporation.
moments.takeaway: Algorithmic quality let a search engine win a crowded market within five years (against AltaVista, Excite, Lycos, Yahoo and Microsoft).

now.title: Search today
now.body: Google handles around 9 billion searches per day. PageRank is only one of hundreds of ranking signals. Generative AI (Bing Chat, Google Bard/Gemini, Perplexity) is reshaping the search interface from 'ten blue links' to conversational answers. The economic model — advertising — has remained central since the introduction of AdWords (2000) and AdSense (2003).
now.open_questions: How does search change when answers replace links? Source attribution, monetisation and information quality all need new frameworks.

items.reflection: Two PhD students built the algorithm that organised the web. The financial scale that followed (Alphabet market cap > $2 trillion) is staggering relative to the original computer-science problem.

moments.title: iPhone launch
moments.body: On 9 January 2007 Jobs unveils the iPhone at Macworld. It combines a touchscreen smartphone, iPod and internet device, running OS X. It launches with no SDK for third-party apps — Jobs initially preferred web apps.
moments.takeaway: The smartphone existed before the iPhone (BlackBerry, Windows Mobile, Symbian); the iPhone redefined what it was.

moments.title: App Store opens
moments.body: On 10 July 2008 the App Store launches with 500 apps. By 2024 there were over 1.8 million apps. The 30%/15% revenue share model becomes the basis of platform economics for the next decade.
moments.takeaway: App stores turned smartphones into developer platforms with a controlled distribution channel.

moments.title: Android and the open alternative
moments.body: HTC Dream (T-Mobile G1) ships with Android in October 2008. Android's open licensing — installed by many manufacturers (Samsung, Xiaomi, Huawei) — eventually gives it the majority of global smartphone market share.
moments.takeaway: Two distinct strategies (closed integrated vs open licensed) co-exist; the platform/handset bifurcation echoes the 1980s PC/Mac split.

now.title: Mobile-first today
now.body: Around 7 billion smartphones globally; ~85% of internet users access via mobile. App stores have come under regulatory pressure (EU Digital Markets Act 2022 forces app store competition on iOS in 2024). Mobile shaped UI conventions, network protocols (mobile-optimised HTTP), photography and payment systems.
now.open_questions: What is the next major form factor? AR/VR (Apple Vision Pro 2024, Meta Quest), wearables and voice interfaces compete; none has yet replaced the smartphone.

items.reflection: A single product launch in 2007 redefined consumer computing for at least the next two decades. Platform decisions made at launch (App Store rules, hardware integration) still shape how digital industries operate.
